titles: How a 1993 game ended up on calculators
The tricks that made Doom run on anything
youtube-meta.description:
In 1993 a small team shipped a game on four floppy disks. Its engine faked a 3D world with flat sectors and a very fast renderer.

Thirty years later people run it on calculators, fridges and printers. Here is why that works.

claims.text: In 1993, a small team in Texas shipped a game
no rooms above rooms, no sloped floors
the original source was released in 1997
it only needs about 4 megabytes of memory

hooks.text: A tiny calculator screen flickers, and a demon from 1993 stares back. Somebody just got Doom running on it, again. Before that it ran on printers, on cash registers, even on a pregnancy test. No other game has been squeezed into so many strange machines, and the reason starts with a small team in Texas and four floppy disks.
hooks.firstVisual: A pixel calculator screen flickering to life with a tiny demon face

hooks.text: Why can a game from the early nineties run on a calculator, a printer and even a pregnancy test, while modern games need powerful graphics cards? The answer is not luck or nostalgia. It is a story about clever shortcuts, a renderer built for speed, and a team that gave its code away to everyone who wanted it.
hooks.firstVisual: A row of odd devices on a shelf, each with a question mark on its screen

hooks.text: Doom needs only about 4 megabytes of memory. That is less than a single photo on your phone, and it is the reason the 1993 shooter now runs on calculators, printers and pregnancy tests. When its source code was released in 1997, programmers everywhere started porting it to anything with a screen and a chip.
hooks.firstVisual: A giant pixel counter ticking up to 4 MB next to a tiny chip
